Cast
KAST
v.
Old Norse kasta, “to throw, hurl.” Renders many Hebrew and Greek verbs of throwing, casting down, casting out, and casting upon; principally the Greek ballō, “to throw,” ekballō, “to cast out,” and epirhiptō, “to cast upon” (1 Pet 5:7).

Biblical Definition

Cast, in the King James Bible, is one of the most freighted verbs in Scripture, carrying a dozen distinct biblical actions according to its preposition and object. To cast out is the verb of exorcism: Christ casts out devils with a word, the disciples are given authority to cast them out, the demons depart at His command. To cast down is to bring low: casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God—the believer’s offensive weapon against speculative pride. To cast off is the act of God in repudiation: Israel feared the LORD had cast them off forever, and Romans 11 returns the question, hath God cast away his people? God forbid. To cast lots is to seek the divine arbitration of an uncertain matter: the apostles cast lots for Judas’s replacement; the disposing of the lot is wholly of the LORD. To cast away is to forfeit: cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward. To cast in one’s lot with another is to throw in one’s portion with theirs (Prov 1:14). And, supremely for the believer’s daily life, to cast upon is the verb of 1 Peter 5:7: casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. The picture is decisive and active: a deliberate throwing of one’s burdens onto Another, not a vague hope that He notices them. The casting is the disposition of the heart in prayer: every anxiety identified, named, and thrown by an act of the will onto the broad shoulders of the Father who has shown He can bear them. The same verb gathers up the great eschatological actions of God: the devil cast into the lake of fire, death and hell cast into the lake of fire, every name not written in the book of life cast in with them. Cast is therefore one of the Bible’s decisive verbs: it does not negotiate, drift, or wish; it throws.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CAST as to throw, fling, or send; to throw down or to throw with violence; to direct or turn, as the eye; to throw out or eject, as from a place.

expand to see more

CAST, v.t. — 1. To throw, fling, or send; that is, to drive from, by force, as from the hand, or from an engine. Cast thy bread upon the waters (Eccl 11:1). 2. To throw down or to throw with violence. 3. To direct or turn, as the eye; to throw the sight. 4. To throw out or eject, as from a place. 5. To deposit, as a vote. 6. To compute; to reckon, as accounts. 7. In scripture, to lay aside, as a hindrance; to throw upon another, as a burden; to throw away, as worthless.

CASTING, ppr. — Throwing; flinging; sending; computing; turning; rejecting; ejecting; casting upon.

Key Scripture

1 Peter 5:7 — "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you."

2 Corinthians 10:5 — "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ."

Romans 11:1-2 — "I say then, Hath God cast away his people? God forbid... God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew."

Hebrews 10:35 — "Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward."

Modern Corruption

The believer’s biblical casting is corrupted by the chronic-anxiety register of the age, in which the burden is endlessly carried in the hand and never thrown by the soul onto the Father—and by the half-cast that briefly throws and then takes back, restoring the worry to the hand at the next provocation.

expand to see more

1 Peter 5:7 is one of Scripture’s most commonly misread verses. Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you is not an encouragement to be less anxious in the abstract; it is the command to perform a deliberate, willed action: a casting—an actual throwing—of the burden, by name and in detail, onto the Father who has invited the throw. The chronic-anxiety register of the contemporary believer collapses the verse into vague reassurance and never performs the casting. The burden remains in the hand. The worry persists, even while the verse is quoted. The cure is the act itself: the deliberate prayer, often spoken aloud, often listed by name, in which the anxieties are identified, surrendered, and committed, with the express purpose of leaving them with God and not picking them back up. The verse does not say be casting; it commands a casting that has a definite shape and a definite end.

The companion corruption is the half-cast, in which the soul throws the burden in prayer in the morning and takes it back at the first provocation in the afternoon. The pattern repeats: cast at devotions, retrieve at frustration, cast again at bedtime, retrieve at the next worried thought. The discipline of casting includes the discipline of refusing to retrieve. The Lord is at hand. Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. The peace is given not to the soul that casts and re-casts the same burden hourly, but to the soul that casts and then lets the peace of God do its garrisoning work. The verb cast is decisive; the saint’s practice of it must be decisive too.

Hebrew Roots

Greek ballō (to throw), ekballō (to cast out), epirhiptō (to cast upon—1 Pet 5:7); Hebrew shālak (to throw, cast) and yārah (to throw, shoot)—a decisive throwing of burdens onto God, devils out of the soul, and high imaginations down to captivity.

expand to see more

Greek ballō (G906) — to throw, cast (the base verb).

Greek ekballō (G1544) — to cast out (exorcism, expulsion).

Greek epirhiptō (G1977) — to cast upon (1 Pet 5:7, “casting all your care upon him”).

Hebrew shālak (H7993) — to throw, cast, fling.
